claim: The AWS-managed private hosted zone for an interface endpoint works only within the VPC that has the endpoint, so for centralized endpoints you turn off the automatic private DNS option, create your own Route 53 private hosted zone with an alias record to the endpoint, and associate it with the other VPCs.
question: Why does the managed private DNS of an interface endpoint not work for spoke VPCs?

values.display: disable the option that automatically creates the private DNS

evidence.quote: The managed PHZ only works within the VPC with the interface endpoint. In our setup, when we want spoke VPCs to be able to resolve VPC endpoint DNS hosted in a centralized VPC, the managed PHZ won’t work.

To overcome this, disable the option that automatically creates the private DNS when an interface endpoint is created. Next, manually create a Route 53 private hosted zone matching the service endpoint name and add an Alias record with the full AWS service endpoint name pointing to the interface endpoint.
You associate this private hosted zone with other VPCs within the Landing Zone.

claim: With VPC sharing, the VPC owner shares one or more subnets with other accounts (participants); participants can view, create, modify and delete their own application resources in the shared subnets but not those of other participants or the owner.
question: What can participants do in a shared VPC subnet?

values.display: shares one or more subnets with other accounts
Participants cannot view, modify, or delete resources that belong to other participants

evidence.quote: In this model, the account that owns the VPC (owner) shares one or more subnets with other accounts (participants). After a subnet is shared, the participants can view, create, modify, and delete their application resources in the subnets shared with them. Participants cannot view, modify, or delete resources that belong to other participants or the VPC owner.

claim: Sharing subnets uses the implicit routing within a VPC for applications that need a high degree of interconnectivity and share a trust boundary, which reduces the number of VPCs you create and manage while separate accounts keep billing and access control.
question: When is VPC sharing an alternative to connecting many VPCs?

evidence.quote: You can share your VPC subnets to use the implicit routing within a VPC for applications that require a high degree of interconnectivity and are within the same trust boundaries. This reduces the number of VPCs that you create and manage, while using separate accounts for billing and access control.

claim: A benefit of VPC sharing is lower cost, because there are no data transfer charges between instances that belong to different accounts within the same Availability Zone.
question: Is data transfer between accounts in a shared VPC subnet charged within an Availability Zone?

values.display: no data transfer charges between instances belonging to different accounts within the same Availability Zone

evidence.quote: Lower costs — no data transfer charges between instances belonging to different accounts within the same Availability Zone

claim: Sharing VPCs is useful when network isolation between teams does not need to be strictly managed by the VPC owner but the account-level users and permissions must be.
question: When is VPC sharing a suitable design?

values.display: network isolation between teams does not need to be strictly managed by the VPC owner

evidence.quote: Sharing VPCs is useful when network isolation between teams does not need to be strictly managed by the VPC owner, but the account level users and permissions must be.
